claims.text: The two groups show identical attack mechanics: each source repeatedly attempts SSH logins with a short, tightly‑spaced burst of failed root or invalid‑user passwords followed by an immediate “Received disconnect … Bye Bye” message that terminates the session.

In Group 183.62.140.253 the cadence is roughly one attempt every 2–3 seconds from 10:54 to 11:04, targeting first a non‑existent user (zhangyan), then several distinct invalid usernames (dff) and finally dozens of root attempts before the pattern repeats at 11:04; this demonstrates a sustained brute‑force sweep that lasts over ten minutes.

Group 187.141.143.180 exhibits an almost identical timing profile—six failed root attempts within the first minute, then a second wave of three invalid‑user attempts at 09:19 – 09:20—but it compresses the entire activity into a tighter nine‑minute window and ends shortly after the final disconnect.

Both sources therefore share the same root‑cause hypothesis: they are part of an automated, credential‑stuffing campaign that uses scripted password‑guessing against SSH, deliberately aborts each connection with a “Bye Bye” signal to avoid detection, and cycles through many source IPs (or rotates payloads) while maintaining a consistent low‑and‑slow burst pattern.

The more anomalous attacker is 183.62.140.253 because its activity persists longer, includes an initial probe of a non‑existent user before moving to root, and shows a higher volume of repeated failed attempts across a broader time span, indicating a more aggressive and less constrained brute‑force effort compared with the shorter, tightly clustered bursts seen from 187.141.143.180.
